title: Telogen effluvium
summary: Diffuse shedding of club hairs 2–3 months after a trigger. Reassure, find reversible causes, and cross-link pattern hair loss rather than duplicating AGA photo sets.

glance.think: Sudden increase in hairs in the brush or shower, diffuse thinning, no bald patches — often 2–3 months after illness, childbirth or a new drug.
glance.engine: A stressor synchronises many anagen follicles into telogen; club hairs shed together weeks later.
glance.backbone: Identify the trigger, check thyroid/ferritin when indicated, reassure that acute TE usually settles in 6–12 months; treat coexistent pattern loss separately.
glance.never_miss: Patchy loss, scale, or lost ostia are not TE — rethink AA, tinea or scarring alopecia.

what: **Telogen effluvium (TE)** is non-scarring **diffuse** shedding of telogen (club) hairs. Acute TE follows a trigger by about **2–3 months**. Chronic TE lasts beyond 6 months.

**Androgenetic (pattern) hair loss** is the other common diffuse-looking thinning of mid-life — full UK IP detail and Module 6 Week 6 photos live on [androgenetic alopecia](condition:androgenetic-alopecia). This page only sketches the DDx so Week 3 teaching stays joined up without duplicating that photo set.

list: Classic triggers: high fever, COVID/flu-like illness, major surgery, postpartum (including when stopping breastfeeding), crash diets, haemorrhage, new drugs (retinoids, anticoagulants, antithyroid, beta-blockers, some anticonvulsants — check BNF), severe stress.
Iron deficiency, thyroid disease and other metabolic insults.
Chronic TE: ongoing trigger or idiopathic; overlap with female pattern loss is common.
Diffuse thinning; parted hair looks thinner; **no discrete bald patch**.
Increased daily shed; club hairs with a white bulb on the brush (photo teaching: D10).
Pull test: many club hairs come out easily when active.
Scalp skin looks normal; ostia preserved.
Pattern loss is gradual miniaturisation over years (male temples/vertex; female crown with widened part, frontal hairline usually kept).
Management (minoxidil, male finasteride MHRA mood warnings, etc.) is covered on the [androgenetic alopecia](condition:androgenetic-alopecia) page, with its own photo gallery.
History timed to a trigger 2–3 months earlier.
Examine for patches, scale, inflammation, pattern miniaturisation.
Bloods when indicated: FBC, ferritin, TFT (± others guided by history).
Child with a scaly patch → mycology (tinea), not TE.

head: Look-alike
Clues
rows: Exclamation hairs, yellow dots, rapid patches

list: Reassure: acute TE usually regrows over **6–12 months** once the trigger has passed; shedding can look alarming but follicles are alive.
Correct reversible causes (iron if deficient, thyroid replacement optimisation, review culprit drugs with the original prescriber).
Gentle hair care; avoid crash diets; camouflage if wanted.
Do not promise “hair vitamins” as evidence-based cure-alls.
If patterned miniaturisation coexists, manage as on the AGA page.
Refer if diagnostic doubt, progressive patterned loss with virilisation, scarring signs, or severe distress.

red_flags: Virilisation or sudden severe FPHL → endocrine/tumour pathways.
Patchy, scaly or shiny bald areas — not TE.
pearls: Postpartum shedding is physiological — counsel antenatally when possible.
Teaching grid: TE (D09) vs FPHL (D06) vs extensive AA — different time courses and trichoscopy.
